correctness.rationale: For every nondegenerate planar triangle and positive prism height, the five-facet offset interval follows exactly from two triangular-face and three rectangular-face projection ranges. The positive-part decomposition integrates over S^2 to the proposed angular formula. Cauchy width gives denominator π(L+2h), and integrating edge crossings gives expected count (4L+6h)/(L+2h). As N is always 3,4,5, the triangle–pentagon gap follows exactly. A six-direction support-order partition and a differentiated explicit antiderivative eliminate the remaining angular quadrature. The included checker verifies this against independent Simpson integrations, complete edge-cut offset subdivisions, and correctly sampled random affine planes. Limits: code tests are finite, but the proof works for all parameters.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Wang proves the tiling property, not a measure-theoretic section law. A five-faced right rectangular pyramid has 5 vertices and 8 edges, whereas the triangular prism has 6 vertices and 9 edges; one cannot specialize its geometric parameter family to obtain all triangular prisms. Mean-square directional width is a different statistic. Voss and Ohser–Mücklich are genuine plausible ancestors of the integral-geometric method; their accessible abstracts neither state nor demonstrate implication of the present explicit law. Unavailable full texts prevent definitive historical priority.

value.rationale: The canonical right triangular prism is a five-faced but non-pyramidal polyhedron, and the family spans every base shape and aspect ratio. The result determines all three invariant-plane section frequencies in finite elementary terms, rather than one isolated numerical example; especially, the unexpected strict gap Pr(triangle)-Pr(pentagon)=2h/(L+2h) loses every base-shape parameter while Pr(pentagon) retains nontrivial base-shape dependence. This supplies a structural geometric invariant and an exact benchmark for stereological inference and section sampling, beyond routine normalization or a numerical table.
